This lack of transparency is particularly problematic in critical fields like healthcare, where trust in a model's predictions is paramount. As a result, the explainability of machine learning (ML) models, as well as other complex models, has become a key area of focus. Efforts to improve model explainability often involve experimenting with AI systems and approximating their behavior through interpretable surrogate mechanisms. However, these procedures can be resource‐intensive. Optimal experimental design (OED), which seeks to maximize the information obtained from a limited number of observations, offers promising methods for improving the efficiency of these explainability techniques. To demonstrate this potential, we explore Local Interpretable Model‐agnostic Explanations (LIME), a widely used method introduced in 2016. LIME provides explanations by generating new data points near the instance of interest and passing them through the model. While effective, this process can be computationally expensive, especially when predictions are costly or require many samples. LIME is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of models and datasets. In this work, we focus on models involving tabular data, regression tasks, and linear models as interpretable local approximations. By utilizing optimal design of experiments' techniques, we reduce the number of function evaluations of the complex model, thereby reducing the computational effort of LIME by a substantial amount. We consider this modified version of LIME to be energy‐efficient, and thus preferable.

Dysarthria is a neurological speech disorder characterized by impaired motor control of speech production, resulting in reduced intelligibility. It commonly arises in the context of neurodegenerative conditions, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and cerebral palsy. The development of deep learning systems for dysarthria assessment is hindered by the scarcity of annotated data, which restricts the ability of models to generalize to unseen speakers. This study proposes a cross-corpus diffusion-based data augmentation strategy for improving automatic speech intelligibility classification from dysarthric speech. A Grad-TTS model is trained on dysarthric speakers from the TORGO dataset and used to synthesize the vocabulary of UA-Speech, producing speaker-conditioned samples intended to transfer pathological acoustic traits across corpora. The proposed strategy is evaluated both independently and in combination with conventional signal-level augmentation using ResNet-50 and ResNet-152 classifiers in binary and four-class intelligibility classification tasks. The results indicate that cross-corpus synthetic augmentation improves average performance and that, in most settings, its integration with conventional augmentation yields further gains, suggesting that the two strategies introduce complementary forms of variability.

BackgroundDigital technologies are promoted to support sustainability transitions, yet their contribution depends on how they are appropriated in activity rather than on technical performance alone.ObjectiveThis article examines the role of technologies in socio-ecological transitions through an activity-centred ergonomics perspective. Drawing on the instrumental approach, it analyses how digital and precision technologies become-or fail to become-instruments for activity in two sectors targeted by sustainability policies: domestic energy management and agriculture.MethodsThe study combines a longitudinal analysis of smart-grid interfaces (SOLENN project) and a cross-case synthesis of four precision agriculture technology (PAT) studies. Although the contexts differ, both are analysed using the same framework grounded in activity-centred ergonomics and the instrumental approach, focusing on epistemic, pragmatic, reflexive, and interpersonal mediations. This framework enables the identification of mechanisms of technology appropriation across sustainability contexts.ResultsTechnological effects do not depend on technical performance alone, but on appropriation processes and instrumental mediations. In domestic energy management, a minority of households stabilised smart-grid interface use when knowledge, motivation, and monitoring practices were present. In agriculture, technologies can support precision, comfort, and temporal flexibility, but also generate reliability work, cognitive load, and transformations in relations with living systems. Across both contexts, findings reveal mechanisms linking use to activity and appropriation.ConclusionsThe findings challenge techno-solutionist approaches by showing that sustainable transitions depend less on technological deployment than on conditions enabling activity. They support a milieu-centred design approach integrating activity, health, collective regulation, and relationships with living environments as sustainability criteria.

This article presents a systematic literature review on the use of emerging technologies in education, with the aim of analyzing their integration into teaching practice and their contribution to improving teaching and learning processes. The literature search was conducted in high-impact, indexed scientific databases, such as Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), Lantidex, SciELO, and Redalyc, covering publications from 2020 to 2025. A total of 836 published scientific articles were retrieved, from which, through a rigorous screening process and application of inclusion and exclusion criteria, 90 articles, both theoretical and empirical, relevant to the review's objectives were selected. The results show a sustained increase in scientific production, particularly since 2020, with a strong emphasis on the use of artificial intelligence, digital platforms, and virtual learning environments. However, the studies analyzed agree that the effectiveness of these technologies depends largely on teachers' pedagogical and digital skills, as well as the existence of clear pedagogical models and ongoing teacher training. Challenges related to the digital divide, resistance to change, and ethical considerations linked to the responsible use of emerging technologies are also identified. It is concluded that their effective integration requires a critical, ethical, and inclusive pedagogical approach aimed at improving the quality of education.

Unsafe behaviors by construction personnel are the primary cause of construction accidents. How to rationally allocate management resources within limited constraints is a core challenge in construction safety management. This study develops and validates a workflow framework integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) and Agent-Based Modeling (ABM), termed LLM-ABM, aimed at achieving intelligent focusing of management strategies and automated interpretation of simulation results. First, an ABM model was constructed in the context of petroleum engineering to analyze the association between different management resource allocations and the evolutionary outcomes of unsafe behaviors under this specific engineering scenario. Second, a complete response surface comprising 231 combinations with a step size of 0.05 was constructed as an evaluation benchmark. On this basis, a manually designed search framework-guided two-round iterative search flow of the LLM-ABM was developed, and ten rounds of independent comparative experiments were conducted against random search to evaluate its strategy-focusing capability. Subsequently, the simulation results were fed into the LLM, and three experts were invited to evaluate the quality of the generated reports from the perspectives of data fidelity, logical coherence, and recommendation actionability. The comparison of the four typical strategies showed that, under the current model settings, active management was associated with a lower mean unsafe personnel ratio (J = 8.05%) and a lower peak unsafe personnel ratio (Pmax = 10.43%), while the balanced strategy was associated with maintaining late-stage average safe personnel ratio (Slate = 60.63%). In terms of strategy focusing, under the current discrete grid with a step size of 0.05 and fixed ABM model settings, the Top-10% hit rate of LLM-ABM reached 20.00%, numerically higher than the 9.50% of random search. Moreover, the final selected strategies exhibit better global rankings on the discrete grid with lower variance. Although this difference did not reach statistical significance due to the limited number of trials, the large effect size preliminarily suggests that LLM-ABM has the potential to focus search resources on high-quality strategy regions. Regarding report generation, expert evaluations yielded scores of 0.95 for data fidelity, 0.87 for logical coherence, and 0.85 for recommendation actionability. This study preliminarily demonstrates that the LLM-ABM workflow possesses the potential to focus search on high-quality strategy regions under a limited budget, as well as the feasibility of transforming structured simulation data into traceable management recommendations, providing a complete technical pathway of “generation–evaluation–feedback–interpretation” for construction safety management in petroleum engineering.

BACKGROUND: Accurately predicting the mode of delivery is a significant challenge in obstetrics, with implications for maternal healthcare planning, resource allocation, and personalized patient counseling. While machine learning offers promising predictive capabilities, the selection of relevant clinical and socioeconomic risk factors from vast possibilities remains a critical and nontrivial step that directly affects model performance and clinical utility. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to (1) predict the mode of delivery (vaginal vs. cesarean) using machine learning algorithms and (2) identify the key risk factors influencing delivery mode prediction. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted on eligible pregnant women who delivered at Bent-Al-Huda Hospital in Bojnourd, Iran. A hybrid feature identification approach was employed: large language models (LLMs) initially proposed 63 potential risk factors. Through iterative refinement involving domain experts and assessment of data availability and frequency, this list was consolidated to 35 final variables for modeling. Machine learning algorithms, including multilayer perceptron (MLP), decision tree, naïve Bayes, and support vector machine (SVM), were applied to build predictive models. RESULTS: Among all models, SVM showed the best performance using all features, achieving an accuracy of 94.8% and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.94. Decision tree analysis identified previous cesarean section history, insurance type, and fetal presentation as the three most important predictive factors. After excluding 40 women with prior cesarean delivery, SVM maintained robust performance with accuracy of 94.3% and an AUC of 0.92. Using antenatal features only, MLP achieved the highest accuracy before and after excluding women with previous cesarean section (92.9% and 92.2%), while SVM also showed the highest discriminative ability (accuracy 92.4%, AUC 0.90 and accuracy 91.3%, AUC 0.87, respectively). CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that combining expert knowledge with LLMs enables effective risk factor identification and that careful feature selection allows the proposed model to predict delivery type with high accuracy.

Large Language models have revolutionised educational approaches across the knowledge spectrum, infusing innovative teaching methods that prioritise student engagement in classroom activities. This article focuses on LLM models in education-centric settings with a teacher focus, aiming to facilitate academic activities. The framework focuses on the key features of the following AI tool platforms: Khanmigo, Diffit, Brisk Teach AI, and eduaide. The study integrated an autoethnographic approach, applied the active learning theory, and Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK) as the theoretical framework, aligned with the study's context. Key teaching functional features of these tools are assessed under the theme: accessibility, open and paid features, user interface, language adaptability, forms of generated content, and assessment. The analysis revealed that these LLM platforms had practical functional features for rationalising teachers' academic activities. It also highlights the importance of educators' roles in integrating AI-generated material thoughtfully for effective teaching and learning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is progressively transforming higher education by incorporating tools capable of supporting teaching, learning, personalization, and feedback. However, its adoption poses challenges related to teacher competencies, technological infrastructure, and the need to establish ethical guidelines for its use. Objective: To analyze the use of artificial intelligence in higher education based on recent scientific evidence. Methodology: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The search was performed in the Scopus, Web of Science, and SciELO databases using search terms in Spanish and English. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 34 articles published between 2024 and 2025 were selected for analysis. Results: The reviewed studies showed that AI-based tools, particularly ChatGPT, can promote pedagogical innovation, personalized learning, and academic feedback. Opportunities were also identified to optimize specific educational activities and expand possibilities for student support. However, limitations persist regarding insufficient teacher training, digital infrastructure and connectivity gaps, and the absence of robust institutional mechanisms for ethical governance. Conclusions: AI has the potential to strengthen teaching and learning processes in higher education, provided that its integration is accompanied by inclusive institutional policies, continuous teacher training, and guidelines promoting the critical, responsible, and ethical use of these technologies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This systematic review examined the applications, outcomes, challenges, and ethical considerations of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in upper secondary education. Studies published between 2022 and August 2026 were searched in Google Scholar, SciELO, Redalyc, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 32 unique empirical studies, examined through an integrative qualitative synthesis. Applications included writing, language learning, mathematics, science, programming, tutoring, and feedback. Findings were heterogeneous, including positive, null, negative, and mixed outcomes. Perceived usefulness and AI-assisted performance do not necessarily indicate independent learning. Key challenges involved cognitive dependence, reliability, equity, academic integrity, and privacy. The educational potential of GenAI depends on pedagogical design and approaches that preserve learner autonomy and critical thinking. Further comparative studies assessing unassisted performance are needed to clarify its effects on learning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: New research papers are published every day, and students and researchers cannot search, read, compare and summarize the relevant ones by hand without losing a lot of time. Generative AI tools, mainly large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), natural language processing (NLP) and AI agents, could cut some of that effort by finding papers, writing summaries, answering specific research questions and pulling out key findings. This paper looks at five works that run from Kitchenham's systematic review method to the LitLLM toolkit and compares their methods, findings and limitations. Six gaps came out of that comparison. Models sometimes invent things and cannot compare papers well. Large collections slow them down. Specialised fields are another weak spot, and they never show how they reached an answer. In the end a person has to check the result anyway. The paper then proposes an eight-stage conceptual framework that goes from database collection through NLP, retrieval, LLM reasoning and generative summarization to a final analysis report, along with evaluation measures and ethical points. The framework is only a concept; it has not been built or benchmarked.

The 2021 WHO CNS tumor classification marked a fundamental shift in neuro-oncology: molecular markers rather than histological appearance now define glioma diagnosis and guide treatment. Yet, in clinical practice the molecular information that matters most to a surgeon—IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion, and methylation class—typically arrives days to weeks after the operation it was meant to inform. Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to close that gap. Over the past several years, a growing body of work has demonstrated that AI models can extract diagnostically relevant molecular and histological information from data sources available in the operating room, in real time, at the point of surgical decision-making. In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art intraoperative AI models available to neurosurgeons during brain tumor resections. They examine AI-augmented approaches to established intraoperative techniques, such as cryosection and fluorescence-guided surgery, before turning to novel technologies including nanopore sequencing and stimulated Raman histology (SRH). The authors conclude by discussing barriers to widespread clinical adoption and what lies ahead for this field. For cryosection, models such as LGNet and the Cryosection Histopathology Assessment and Review Machine (CHARM) have demonstrated strong performance on intraoperative discrimination of primary CNS lymphoma and molecular subtyping of glioma, respectively, with CHARM achieving areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88–0.93 across glioma subtypes. In fluorescence-guided surgery, hyperspectral imaging combined with machine learning has enabled classification of tumor type, grade, and IDH mutation based on the 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) signal with up to 93% accuracy, extracting molecular information from a modality already present in the operating room. For nanopore-based methylation classification, ensemble models such as Rapid Nanopore Brain Intraoperative Classification (ROBIN) have achieved 90% concordance with the final diagnosis prospectively in under 2 hours. In SRH, foundation models for infiltration detection now outperform FLAIR, contrast enhancement, and 5-ALA fluorescence in identifying tumor margins, while molecular classification models have achieved over 90% glioma subtype accuracy in multi-institutional cohorts. At the single-cell level, morphometric profiling of SRH images has revealed nuclear features distinguishing IDH-mutant from IDH-wildtype tumors, opening new avenues for interpretability. Despite this progress, widespread adoption remains limited by the absence of randomized clinical trials demonstrating patient-level benefit. Addressing this gap and realizing the potential of multimodal AI systems that integrate imaging, pathology, and molecular data represent critical next steps for the field.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in healthcare, but their utility in plastic surgery and skin cancer management remains in contention. Furthermore, the comparative performance of LLMs in the setting of skin cancer surgery is unclear. This study assessed four widely used LLMs and comparatively evaluated their relevance, accuracy, and clinical representativeness. Methods: This prospective study evaluated six standardised skin cancer prompts submitted to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Copilot. Specialist plastic surgeons assessed textual responses for relevance and accuracy, and generated images for clinical representativeness and accuracy. Readability and DISCERN scores were also assessed. Results: All four LLMs produced highly relevant textual responses, with relevance scores ranging from 4 to 5, while accuracy scores ranged from 3 to 5. ChatGPT and Copilot achieved the highest individual accuracy scores. Only ChatGPT and Gemini generated images. ChatGPT demonstrated greater clinical representativeness and accuracy across all image prompts. ChatGPT produced the most linguistically complex responses, while Copilot produced the most readable outputs. All models generated text requiring at least a high-school level of education. Claude achieved the highest mean DISCERN score (43.67), followed by ChatGPT (40.33), Copilot (36.00), and Gemini (35.67). Conclusions: In this exploratory comparison, contemporary LLM-based platforms produced relevant and largely accurate skin cancer surgery information, but differed in image generation, readability, and information quality. The generated images depicted predominantly lighter skin tones, which warrants greater input from more diverse patient populations, and outputs should be used alongside clinician review. Larger studies using patient-specific scenarios and diverse skin tones are needed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Occupational health is frequently undervalued and is often involved only when workplace difficulties have escalated or sickness absence has become prolonged. This book argues for a more proactive and clinically grounded approach to occupational health consultations, one that considers not only whether an individual is fit for work but also whether the workplace is fit for health. The book integrates the biopsychosocial model with cognitive behavioural reasoning to provide a structured way of understanding how biological, psychological and workplace factors interact to influence functioning at work. Particular emphasis is placed on assessing psychosocial factors, including how individuals interpret their symptoms, how these interpretations influence behaviour and confidence, and how workplace demands and supports shape work ability. Central to the approach is a clear five-part formulation that considers presenting concerns, vulnerabilities, triggers, maintaining factors and strengths. This formulation informs focused, work-related strategies to improve function and support earlier engagement with emerging health concerns. Written for occupational health professionals and others working at the interface of work and health, the book reframes the occupational health consultation as a meaningful clinical encounter that supports understanding, prevention and functional change in the workplace.

This introduction sets the conceptual and contextual foundation for the edited volume by tracing the development of reflective practice (RP) in second language education (SLE) and examining its renewed significance in the digital era. It first situates RP within the work of Dewey and Schön and discusses its relevance for language teachers as thinking professionals who interpret complex classroom, institutional and sociocultural realities. The introduction then considers how digital technologies, including learning management systems, Eportfolios, video platforms, online communities, corpus tools, social media, chatbots, and generative AI, are reshaping the conditions under which teachers document, analyze and make sense of their professional experiences. While acknowledging the potential of these tools to extend and support reflection, it also highlights important concerns related to superficial engagement, performativity, surveillance, dependency and decontextualized feedback. The chapter outlines the main contributions of the volume, introduces its three-part organization, and argues for a human-centered, ethical, context-sensitive and professionally meaningful approach to technology-mediated RP in SLE.

Transdermal drug delivery systems (TDDS) provide a non-invasive alternative to oral and injectable administration; however, their clinical utility remains limited by the formidable barrier properties of the stratum corneum, which restrict the delivery of many therapeutic agents, particularly hydrophilic and high-molecular-weight molecules. Invasomes, composed of phospholipids, ethanol, and terpenes, have emerged as highly deformable nanovesicular carriers capable of enhancing skin permeation through synergistic lipid fluidization and vesicular flexibility. This review provides a comprehensive and updated overview of invasome-based transdermal drug delivery, distinguishing itself from previous reviews by integrating recent advances in formulation strategies, physicochemical characterization, penetration mechanisms, therapeutic applications, smart and hybrid invasomes, computational formulation design, regulatory considerations, and translational challenges. The review critically discusses the influence of formulation variables, including phospholipid composition, ethanol content, terpene type, and drug physicochemical properties, on vesicle characteristics, stability, encapsulation efficiency, and biological performance. Furthermore, recent in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo studies collectively demonstrate that invasomes significantly enhance skin permeation, drug deposition, bioavailability, and therapeutic efficacy compared with conventional vesicular systems while maintaining favorable safety profiles. Emerging innovations, including stimuli-responsive invasomes, microneedle-assisted delivery, artificial intelligence-guided formulation optimization, and molecular modeling, are also highlighted as promising approaches for next-generation transdermal therapies. Despite encouraging preclinical evidence, challenges related to large-scale manufacturing, long-term stability, regulatory standardization, and clinical validation remain to be addressed. Overall, this review provides a current and translational perspective on invasome technology and highlights its potential as a versatile nanovesicular platform for future clinical transdermal drug delivery.

The electrochemical performance of lithium-ion batteries is strongly governed by the complex three-dimensional architecture of porous electrodes. While recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have enabled realistic reconstruction of battery microstructures, existing approaches primarily focus on reproducing morphology or correlating manufacturing parameters with structural characteristics, providing limited control over transport-relevant properties. In this work, we develop a physics-constrained conditional generative adversarial network (PC-cGAN) for the inverse generation of LiNi 0.5 Mn 0.3 Co 0.2 O 2 , NMC532 cathode microstructures conditioned on target physical descriptors. The framework integrates a physical constraint network that enforces porosity, active-material volume fraction, and tortuosity during training, enabling direct generation of microstructures consistent with desired transport characteristics. Beyond morphology reconstruction, the framework also supports inverse microstructure design by mapping user-specified transport properties directly into three-dimensional, physically consistent electrode architectures. This functionality opens a pathway to probe structure-transport relationships that are otherwise challenging to isolate experimentally, while laying the groundwork for AI-enabled digital twins of battery electrodes. Coupling the framework with electrochemical and manufacturing simulations will enable virtual screening of architectures, accelerate optimization cycles, and advance physics-guided battery design with reduced experimental effort.

The digital revolution in India has touched every aspect of human endeavor from as basic as birth registration to Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) assisted scientific research. One of the most basic requirements- education is spurred by EdTech platforms. It offers students several opportunities and simultaneously exposes children to the risks of mass surveillance through data collection. The proliferation of virtual classrooms has enhanced the data collection, processing, and potential misuse of children's sensitive and personal information by the EdTech providers. This raises urgent questions about the legal protections and their adequacy within India's regulatory framework for protection of the children given the recent data commercialization and breaches in maintenance of children's data by Edtech. The aim of the study is to analyse the existing legal framework on the available protection and make recommendations that should feature in the rules that the government may make for the protection of children against the possible misuse by the EdTech companies. The study uses a doctrinal approach whereby the existing law will be analysed to unearth the loopholes in the context of child's right to privacy in EdTech offered classrooms. This analysis is fruitful for policy making in the area by mooting for an oversight mechanism to ensure compliance and fix liability in case of breach on the EdTech platforms.

KONNEX AI – KAI Chat is an intelligent, agentic AI-powered communication platform designed to transform how individuals and businesses interact, connect, and manage digital relationships. Developed by KONNEX INC., KAI Chat leverages large language models (LLMs), natural language processing (NLP), autonomous AI agents, and contextual intelligence to enable personalized conversations, intelligent messaging, automated follow-ups, and cross-platform communication. The platform envisions a personal AI digital twin capable of understanding user preferences, communication styles, and relationship contexts to assist with SMS, email, social messaging, customer engagement, and professional networking. By integrating conversational AI, workflow automation, and human-centered design, KAI Chat aims to advance the next generation of intelligent communication systems, making digital interactions more efficient, personalized, and connected while emphasizing user control, privacy, and responsible AI deployment.

As automated systems become increasingly embedded in everyday consumer technologies, understanding how individual differences shape engagement decisions is critical for supporting users. The present study examined how task-specific expertise influences engagement with an optional GPS assistant across fourteen trials in a simulated map-based navigation task. Ninety-one undergraduate participants were classified as navigational experts or novices by accuracy on a task-specific knowledge test of the simulated maps. As hypothesized, experts engaged the GPS significantly less than novices. Despite the difference in engagement, navigational accuracy did not significantly differ between groups, suggesting that novices engaged the GPS at rates that compensated for their lower expertise bringing their performance to comparable levels of experts. Post-hoc analyses revealed that poorer spatial orientation was associated with greater GPS engagement and lower navigational expertise. These findings suggest individuals may make calibrated and capability driven decisions about their automation engagement.

Abstract Robocalls, spam texts, and scam calls all exploit one design assumption: anyone who knows a phone number, SIP URI, or messaging handle can attempt contact. Once a number is shared with a business, a marketplace seller, a delivery driver, or a directory listing, it becomes a permanent, reusable route, and leaked or brokered contact data keeps that route open for anyone who obtains it. Existing defences answer different questions. STIR/SHAKEN verifies who is calling, not whether that caller is permitted to reach this recipient now. Virtual and masked numbers hide the real number but stay dialable while active. OAuth delegates API access but defines no telecom reachability rules. Spam scoring and call screening judge an attempt only after it has already been routed and signaled. This disclosure describes an authorization-to-reach model that separates knowing a contact identifier from permission to make contact. Each inbound call, message, or notification is held as a candidate request until an enforcement point, such as a session border controller, SIP application server, IMS node, or CPaaS gateway, validates a recipient-scoped grant bound to sender, recipient, purpose or transaction, channel, expiry, attempt quota, revocation epoch, and audience, with replay protection and sender binding so that a copied grant is not a bearer credential. Only then does the phone ring or the message get delivered; otherwise the request is rejected (for example with SIP 403) before any communication takes effect. Three deployment profiles, blocked path, pre-routing authorization, and absent path, allow incremental rollout over existing E.164 numbering, SIP, IMS, and PSTN infrastructure, while emergency calls (911/112) and lawful intercept remain unaffected. The gap grows as AI agents and AI-native 6G networks originate contact at machine speed. The record includes use cases (map and directory enquiries, marketplaces, ride and delivery, AI assistants), a comparison with existing approaches, a candidate grant format, possible STIR/PASSporT, SIP, and OAuth encodings, security and privacy analysis, a 58-question telecom engineering FAQ, and five workflow charts. A reference implementation is publicly available. Its central principle: possession of a communication identifier is not, by itself, permission to communicate. Download the full PDF to review the workflow charts, grant format, deployment profiles, and complete FAQ. Keywords: robocall prevention; spam call blocking; scam calls; SMS spam; caller ID spoofing; STIR/SHAKEN; PASSporT; SIP; IMS; session border controller; CPaaS; number masking; virtual numbers; privacy relay; consent to contact; contact data leakage; telecom fraud prevention; authorization-to-reach; purpose-scoped authorization; revocable grant; capability token; non-bearer token; OAuth RAR; DPoP; replay protection; zero-trust telecom; 6G; IMT-2030; AI-native networks; AI agents; machine-originated traffic; emergency call routing; TCPA; GDPR

The rapid advancement of digital technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), virtual and augmented reality, the Internet of Things (IoT), and the Internet of Everything (IoE), has reshaped human life, raising existential questions and challenging traditional sources of meaning. This study addresses the problem of how these technological transformations affect individuals’ processes of meaning-making and the management of knowledge in the digital era. The aim of this study is to examine the relationship between digital technologies, digital literacy, and knowledge management, with a particular focus on their implications for existential inquiry and meaningful engagement with technology. A rapid review methodology was applied to analyze 18 peer-reviewed studies indexed in Scopus, published between 2010 and 2024. The analysis explored their relevance to existentialism, meaning-making, and human existence in the context of digital technologies. The thematic analysis identified five key themes: AI and existential concerns, technology and human experience, embodied cognition and technology, digital literacy and knowledge management, and technology and meaningful interaction. The findings indicate that digital technologies substantially reshape identity, autonomy, and individuals’ search for meaning, while digital literacy emerges as a central capability for navigating these changes and supporting effective knowledge management. The study highlights important implications for research and practice, suggesting that strengthening digital literacy is essential to foster more meaningful interactions with technology and to mitigate potential negative existential and cognitive effects. Limitations include potential selection biases, reliance on self-reported data, and cultural and socioeconomic constraints that may affect the generalizability of the results.

This chapter examines knowledge graphs as the semantic integration backbone of next-generation research infrastructures. It traces the theoretical distinctions separating knowledge graphs from ontologies and relational schemas, surveys RDF-based storage and federated query architectures, and reviews ontology alignment, embedding-based representation learning, and knowledge graph completion as mechanisms for reconciling heterogeneous data sources. Applications across biomedicine, cultural heritage, bibliometrics, and recommendation are examined alongside the convergence of knowledge graphs with large language models for explainable, grounded reasoning. The chapter concludes by identifying scalability, governance, and provenance challenges facing research infrastructure architects designing federated, cognitively grounded data systems.

Computer-based intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) use Student Modelling and Knowledge Tracing (KT) at the core of adaptive learning environments to model and predict each learner's mastery. While conversational AI improves pedagogical feedback, the core adaptability of ITS ultimately depends on strong Educational Data Mining (EDM) and Learning Analytics (LA) algorithms. Existing literature reviews often conflate frontend instructional AI with backend analytics, leaving a critical gap in synthesizing the computational approaches and predictive systems that drive these intelligent systems. To address this gap, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following PRISMA guidelines, systematically analysing 15 high-quality studies focused only on the computational dimensions of ITS. The results show a clear model shift away from simple traditional probabilistic models towards the latest versions of deep-learning based classic DKT architectures, including context-aware gating and Transformer networks. Learner state representations are also increasingly complex and add behavioural interaction histories rather than simple testing observations of correct or incorrect outcomes. While the validity of these data-driven models continues to be high (particularly in well-structured domains like mathematics), their real-world operational challenges are much harder to resolve, with major technical issues of data sparsity, algorithmic bias, sustainability of pedagogic fit and the diffuse "black-box" of deep neural networks common across the literature. These issues mean that future researches, defined by the authors as the ongoing interaction between the computational and human, should seek to develop explainable AI (XAI) and fairness-aware algorithms that support scalable, trusted human-AI teaming.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Abstract The gap between expert knowledge and layperson understanding often poses challenges to the effective communication of unfamiliar concepts. To address this issue, we introduce a semi‐automated, interactive visual summarization framework with modularity and user control, KnowTI, which leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) and visualization methods to facilitate knowledge transfer. Our approach aims to narrow the knowledge gap of laypersons in comprehending complex information as presented by experts, while remaining engaged, making our solution applicable to a variety of information communication contexts—including, but not limited to, educational videos. We validate the effectiveness of KnowTI through a comparative study with 40 participants, contrasting our approach with traditional video‐based learning. Findings indicate that KnowTI not only enhances knowledge acquisition and engagement, but also supports laypersons in understanding complex, domain‐specific topics, bridging the knowledge gap between experts and non‐experts. All supplementary material, including the code, analysis, and evaluation, is available on GitHub .

Large language models (LLMs) are a double-edged technology. They can serve as learning assistants in programming while simultaneously raising pedagogical and ethical concerns. Programming education researchers have responded by providing guidelines and recommendations on teaching, assessment, and the ethical use of LLMs. Although these developments are welcome, the literature still lacks theory-based frameworks that provide a philosophical grounding for programming pedagogy. This perspective paper addresses this gap by proposing the LLM-Assisted Modern Programming Pedagogy (LAMPP) model. The model aims to provide a theory-informed framework for systematically guiding the integration of LLMs into programming pedagogy. It proposes four design principles encompassing the core components of pedagogy (i.e., teaching, lesson design, engagement, and assessment). Ethics is included as an additional dimension because ethical concerns cut across all aspects of pedagogy. The LAMPP model proposes different mechanisms that may mitigate potential learning losses associated with inappropriate or excessive reliance on LLMs. Future studies should test the effectiveness of these mechanisms. The model may provide a basis for educators, researchers, and policymakers when considering policies, curriculum structures, course outcomes, assessment practices, and ethical guidelines related to programming pedagogy. In summary, it is not about LLM tools themselves but about the pedagogical orchestration of these technologies in programming education.

With the continuous expansion of cross-border agricultural supply chains, reliable food-safety risk screening under decentralized data ownership, heterogeneous sensing equipment, and jurisdiction-dependent, non-stationary regulatory limits pose a fundamental challenge to intelligent inspection systems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an LLM-assisted regulation-aware heterogeneous multimodal federated learning framework that establishes a three-tier decoupling architecture. First, an available-modality and quality-adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically weights RGB images, near-infrared (NIR) spectra, and environmental time-series while enforcing strict zero weighting on unavailable modalities and continuous suppression of degraded observations. Second, a regulation-independent state-prototype collaboration and personalized federated learning strategy is developed on a unified continuous concentration scale, enabling cross-institutional transfer of physical contamination representations while avoiding the use of jurisdiction-dependent compliance labels to define shared prototype groups and preserving client-specific adapters against non-IID drift. Third, offline large language model (LLM) parsing transforms unstructured multi-jurisdictional trade regulations into machine-executable rule bases, which are coupled with an uncertainty-aware risk calibration module to dynamically determine exceedance probabilities and reinspection recommendations without retraining front-end sensing encoders when regulatory standards shift. Experimental evaluations on a multisource maize and aflatoxin B1 screening dataset in a workstation-based federated simulation demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.054±0.002 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.078±0.003, while elevating the area under the curve (AUC) and F1-score to 0.862±0.008 and 0.833±0.009, respectively, reducing the false negative rate (FNR) to 0.121±0.007 (p<0.001). Under severe client heterogeneity and missing-modality scenarios, the proposed approach maintains an AUC of 0.823±0.010 and an F1-score of 0.796±0.011. Ablation and ownership-level analyses assess robustness, calibration (expected calibration error of 0.032), and regulatory adaptation with fixed sensing encoders, providing an end-to-end, traceable decision-support paradigm for international agricultural trade screening.

This study evaluated an open-weight LLM and keyword rules for title/abstract screening of circulating microRNA (miRNA) monitoring biomarker reviews. PubMed and Europe PMC searches returned 3,204 records (1,976 after deduplication). Automated keyword rules excluded 1,222 records; 754 were screened by gpt-oss-120b (n = 628) or gpt-oss-20b (n = 126) at temperature 0. One reviewer labelled 225 records; a second independently labelled a stratified 113-record sample, and 21 disagreements were adjudicated to consensus (2 Include, 3 Maybe, 16 Exclude), serving as the reference, though blinding of the first reviewer to LLM outputs could not be verified. The primary outcome was sensitivity for Include or Maybe against a pre-set threshold of 0.95. The LLM returned Include 173, Maybe 102, and Exclude 479. Against the consensus reference, sensitivity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.77–0.95), specificity 0.90 (95% CI 0.83–0.95), and kappa 0.65 (95% CI 0.54–0.76). Of 100 randomly sampled LLM-excluded records, 5 (5%) were reference-Include; in all five, the LLM's stated reason involved prognostic or clinical-event outcomes rather than drug response, resistance, or toxicity. Among keyword-excluded records, 11/75 (15%) were reference-Include, rising to 11/50 (22%) for the rule 'no human circulating miRNA + treatment context'. The sensitivity point estimate fell below 0.95, but its 95% CI (0.77–0.95) includes 0.95, so this pilot cannot rule out that the threshold is met; keyword pre-filters excluded relevant records at a rate that made them unsafe without audit. In this domain, an LLM can prioritise records but cannot replace human screening. The authors propose clearer outcome criteria, single-model runs, stratified human audits of every automated exclusion, and pre-registered performance thresholds.

This chapter analyzes published work on the use of large language models (LLMs) in smart frameworks for the detection and prevention of cyberbullying across social media, gaming, and learning platforms. The data shows a clear movement from the use of traditional machine learning and earlier deep learning models to the application of LLMs that possess capabilities of understanding and processing context, which allow them to identify and categorize abuses of the online environment that are subtle and implicit, as well as those that use multiple modalities and languages. The literature shows the following recurring themes: use of prompt-engineered LLMs for cyberbullying detection with little or no training; hybrid models that integrate LLMs with classical machine learning; moderation models; and conversational agents for real-time, empathetic abuse interventions. Other themes include increased focus on bias and fairness, explainability, data scarcity, and domain adaptation for high-risk systems and safety. The chapter provides this structure by first assessing foundational literature on automated detection of cyberbullying and toxic language, then LLM-based detection architectures and LLM-enabled prevention and intervention strategies, such as counseling chatbots and bystander aid tools. The subsequent sections integrate the literature on evaluation methodologies, benchmark datasets, and the spatial and temporal adversity and abusive behavior countermeasure robustness, then address the specific ethical, legal, and policy LLM online safety ecosystem deployment issues. This extensive literature review provides a synthesis of the LLM literature on online safety tools, determines converging design strategies and unresolved issues, and articulates design principles for LLM-based tools that promote safer online communities.

Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for oncology decision support, but their performance in colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastases (CRC-PM) remains uncertain. We benchmarked 10 contemporary LLMs against an expert-consensus framework. Methods Forty-eight synthetic vignettes were derived from a 2026 CRC-PM consensus guideline, including 36 primary scenarios and 12 counterfactual scenarios forming six pairs. Each model completed every vignette three times using a frozen zero-shot structured prompt. The primary endpoint was prompt-aligned structured Full concordance; contradiction-only and full-semantic adjudication were sensitivity analyses. Two blinded attending colorectal surgeons, each with 5 years of clinical experience, independently validated the reference classifications. Results Among 1,080 primary responses, structured scoring classified 609 (56.4%) as Full, 117 (10.8%) as Partial, and 354 (32.8%) as Discordant. Model-specific structured Full concordance ranged from 49.1% to 63.0%; neither the Friedman test ( P = .104) nor clustered GEE ( P = .186) supported a robust model effect. Contradiction-only scoring was similar (56.2% Full), whereas full-semantic adjudication reduced Full concordance to 45.5%. Excluding prompt-development scenarios lowered absolute concordance but did not change the inferential conclusion. Expert agreement was 93.8%–97.9% across decision domains (Cohen kappa 0.898–0.948). Counterfactual and metachronous risk-management analyses showed wide uncertainty, and 21 clinically consequential discordance flags arose from five scenarios. Conclusions LLM performance in CRC-PM was sensitive to scoring definition and did not establish a stable between-model hierarchy. Prospective clinician-plus-LLM studies are required before clinical benefit can be inferred.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Product design is a complex, knowledge-based process that balances customer needs with engineering constraints and market realities. While traditional methods such as Quality Function Deployment (QFD) and machine learning (ML) have improved the design process and solutions, they still struggle with flexibility and a deep semantic understanding of design requirements. Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), create new opportunities for intelligent, human-centred support for product design. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review analyzes 1,263 studies published between 2023 and 2026 to answer three questions: (1) how LLMs are applied across design stages, (2) how these systems are evaluated, and (3) what gaps remain. We found that LLMs successfully support design requirements analysis, ideation, and documentation. However, current evaluation methods lack standardized benchmarks for design quality. Persistent challenges remain, including hallucinations, weak domain grounding, tool-integration hurdles, and ethical concerns. To guide future research, we introduce a technical maturity map that highlights current achievements and uninvestigated areas in design systems and suggests a roadmap for applying LLMs in product design.

Through architecture, aesthetics, and material agency, ecological consciousness unfolds as a journey across scales. Thus, this book’s conclusion proposes a final time–space transscalar journey from the Paleolithic cave in France to current lunar and deep-sea explorations aimed at expanding the human condition through artificial intelligence. The ultimate demonstration underscores the urgent need to cherish and reclaim the chirotopian spaces threatened by excessive material abstraction. Therefore, the ordinary spaces within reach, fostered within architectural spaces, can not only propel the construction of a new cosmology that recognizes vibrant matter but also amplify the distinct sensibility that makes us human.

Differentiating Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) respiratory syndromes requires weighing overlapping symptoms together with tongue and pulse findings, a task that most AI systems for TCM perform end-to-end but without an interpretable intermediate representation. In this study, we addressed this gap with LEAF (LLM extraction and multiobjective feature selection), a two-stage modular framework evaluated on 3,253 records covering 14 respiratory syndromes from the TCM-SD benchmark. Its first large language model (LLM) stage extracted a 35-item symptom ontology that was built entirely from public TCM sources; among three interchangeable LLMs, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was ranked as the best, followed by Phi-4 and the TCM domain model BianCang. Its second evolutionary-computation stage benchmarked four multiobjective evolutionary algorithms [non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II), strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm 2 (SPEA2), competitive mechanism-based multiobjective particle swarm optimizer (CMOPSO), and non-dominated sorting differential evolution (NSDE)] over 10 seeds, and they were compared using Friedman’s and Nemenyi’s testing in terms of both classification outcome and search-process quality. The four algorithms showed no significant separation on held-out macro-F1, although NSDE led nominally, and none exceeded the full-feature baseline on point estimates. In contrast, hypervolume differed significantly and favored NSGA-II, the weakest of the four on held-out macro-F1. A four-classifier panel found no algorithm to be significantly different from either the full-feature baseline or a random-feature control, which was significantly outperformed only by the full-feature baseline. Applying NSDE to the remaining two LLM pipelines reproduced the original ranking, and its representative solution was fully attested against the knowledge base of TCM-SD, although not typically so across all the 10 seeds. These results show that an LLM-extraction frontend built exclusively from public knowledge can provide a representation over which evolutionary feature selection cuts the candidate feature set roughly in half without a statistically detectable cost in performance, albeit at a small point-estimate cost; that hypervolume and inverted generational distance are not reliable stand-ins for classification-relevant algorithm selection here; and that a no-gold-standard proxy evaluation can substitute human annotation when expert time is limited. Because both stages plug in and out freely, the framework can absorb stronger components in either stage as they become available.

Generative AI (GenAI) is changing how design students learn, yet little is known about how students’ perceived capability to work with GenAI relates to their learning engagement and motivational self-beliefs, or under which forms of AI dependence this link is weaker. Drawing on social cognitive theory, this cross-sectional study examined self-reported prompt literacy, learning engagement, and two components of the creative self: creative self-efficacy (CSE), a motivational belief in one’s creative capability, and creative personal identity (CPI), the importance of creativity to one’s self-concept. Survey data came from 829 undergraduate art and design students in 40 intact classes at two institutions in mainland China; latent-variable and moderation models accounted for the clustering of students within classes. Self-reported prompt literacy was positively associated with engagement ( β = 0.54), and engagement was positively associated with both CSE ( β = 0.62) and CPI ( β = 0.47). Engagement was more strongly associated with CSE than with CPI (difference = 0.14, 95% CI [0.04, 0.24]) and remained uniquely associated with CPI after CSE was taken into account. When four dimensions of AI dependence were modeled simultaneously, the prompt literacy–engagement association was weaker among students reporting higher cognitive dependence; evidence for loss of control was weaker, and functional and emotional dependence showed no clear unique moderation. All interaction effects were small. The dimensional analysis identified cognitive dependence as the clearest moderator. These cross-sectional, self-reported findings suggest possible boundary conditions for the capability–engagement association and require longitudinal and behavioral testing.

Real-world learning scenarios often exhibit asymmetries between training and inference, where additional or higher-quality information is available only during training. The Learning Under Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm provides a formal framework to study such settings. Despite research interest over the years, the extensive literature on LUPI remains highly fragmented. In this survey, we present a comprehensive and structured overview of research on LUPI and its related formulations. We review 107 papers published between 2009 and 2025 and propose a novel unified taxonomy based on two core dimensions: the underlying machine learning models, spanning both shallow and deep architectures, and the methodological strategies used to integrate privileged information. Additionally, we provide an extensive overview of the various application domains and the particular types of privileged modalities used. We also discuss key insights and open challenges, focusing on how and when privileged information can be effectively leveraged in modern machine learning systems.

The relevance of this study is determined by the fact that, for Level 4 autonomous ships, traditional situational awareness architectures do not comply with Rule 5 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea concerning continuous lookout by all available means, since such ships do not distinguish between random noise, sensor degradation, and cyberattacks. This paper proposes a Level 1 situational awareness architecture consistent with the Endsley model. Sensors are divided into a continuously active core (radar, satellite navigation systems, Automatic Identification System, optical and thermal imaging cameras, microphones, and other systems) and specialized modules (LiDAR, Doppler speed log, sonar). A Sensor Trust Manager with a quality metric and a trust management protocol for navigational information sensors have been developed, combining noise level, deviation from the predicted value, cyberattack (spoofing) detection, and packet loss. The Trust Manager operates a six-state automaton (NOMINAL, DEGRADED, SUSPECT, ISOLATED, RECOVERING, FAILED) with transition hysteresis, ensuring resistance to short-term interference without false sensor isolation. Trust Managers ensure the isolation of unreliable sources before data enter the fusion filters. Thus, only physically reliable and time-consistent data are supplied to complex fusion algorithms (Kalman filters, trackers), which is critical for preventing “contamination” of the target vessel state assessment. The proposed architecture combines compliance with Rule 5, scenario adaptation through the division of sensors into basic and specialized groups, and cyber resilience (spoofing) through signal evaluation based on quality criteria, creating a theoretical basis for certification of Level 4 autonomous marine surface ships in accordance with the requirements of the Code of Safety for Autonomous Surface Ships .

The widespread adoption of mobile devices has driven the development of diverse educational technologies. In this context, Artificial Intelligence-based Mobile Adaptive Learning Systems (AI-based MALS) have emerged as an efficient alternative to complement the teaching and learning process. However, the advancement of these systems is hindered by significant challenges such as insufficient software architectural support, lack of standardization, and inadequate requirements coverage and correctness. Addressing these challenges requires designing high-quality software architectures. Accordingly, research focused on the design, development, and evaluation of software architectures for AI-based MALS is critical from a software engineering standpoint. Although some secondary studies have explored related topics through literature reviews and systematic mapping, no comprehensive secondary review has identified the principal architectural aspects of AI-based MALS design. This study conducts a Literature Review (LR) of software architectures that integrate Artificial Intelligence into Mobile Adaptive Learning Systems. The main objective is to identify and compare the critical aspects of software architectures for proposed AI-based MALS in the specialized literature. The findings highlight several essential elements that software architectures for AI-based MALS should address, including requirements, quality attributes, stakeholders, user services, architectural views and styles, components, and implementation technologies. The primary finding of this study is the absence of a reference software architecture in the reviewed studies that comprehensively addresses the requirements needed to develop AI-based MALS to support adaptive learning in mobile distributed environments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) trajectory planning in dense urban environments requires models that generalize to rare or previously unseen scenario types. Deep neural networks (DNNs) trained on large datasets perform poorly in such data-scarce conditions, while large language models (LLMs) generalize well but lack the numerical precision required for low-level vehicle control. This paper presents a hybrid trajectory planning framework that fuses a finetuned LLM with a multi-branch DNN at the trajectory level and applies a Model Predictive Control (MPC) controller as a final optimization stage. Gemini 1.5 Flash, fine-tuned on 479 labeled scenario-trajectory pairs, generates 15- aypoint trajectory proposals from structured textual scene descriptions. A modular DNN processes the same scene as a numerical input vector and produces a parallel trajectory proposal. The two proposals are fused by a learned trajectory refinement network, and the output is passed to an MPC controller that enforces vehicle dynamics constraints while minimizing a multi-objective cost function. Training relies on a three-step distortion- based augmentation technique, curve distortion, scale distortion, and Gaussian smoothing, that generates semi-realistic trajectory variants from a base dataset of over 70,000 labeled rows, reducing the data volume required for effective DNN training. Evaluation across 200 runs in the CARLA simulator on unseen urban scenarios shows that the MPC-enhanced hybrid model achieves an Average Displacement Error (ADE) of 0.66 m and a Final Displacement Error (FDE) of 1.94 m, corresponding to improvements of 37.7% and 34.3% over the DNN-only baseline. The collision rate (CR) decreases from 3.71% to 2.90%, a 21.8% reduction. These results establish that trajectory-level fusion of LLM semantic reasoning with DNN-based feature extraction delivers measurable accuracy and safety gains in data-efficient autonomous driving conditions. The ADE/FDE improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.001). The collision-rate reduction is a consistent trend across ablations, but it is not statistically significant at n = 200 runs (see Section 4.4).

ABSTRACT Identity‐based Recommendation (IDR) plays a crucial role in modern personalized recommendation systems by leveraging users' identity information and historical interactions to model long‐term user preferences. However, existing IDR methods face three critical challenges: difficulty in fully capturing latent user preference, limited representational capacity, and poor adaptability to cold‐start scenarios. To address these issues, we propose the LLM‐Enhanced Semantic Information Alignment for ID Recommendation (ESIA‐IDR) framework, which systematically integrates semantic features generated by large language models (LLMs) into ID‐based recommendation. ESIA‐IDR first employs LLMs to deeply perceive unstructured textual data, such as user reviews and product descriptions, thereby effectively mining users' latent interest patterns. An independent pretraining mechanism is then applied to optimize the training dynamics of semantic and ID embeddings, mitigating inconsistencies in convergence behavior. Additionally, a feature discretization strategy is adopted to enhance semantic feature compatibility with traditional recommendation pipelines. During the recommendation phase, semantic‐enhanced features and collaborative signals are jointly modeled to achieve robust performance in cold‐start environments. ESIA‐IDR consists of four key components: Semantic and Interest Perception, Semantic Alignment, Discrete Feature Construction, and Recommendation Integration. By combining pretraining, dimensionality reduction, and similarity‐based bucketing, the framework achieves effective alignment between semantic features and ID feature spaces, bridging the semantic‐structural gap and improving user preference modeling accuracy. Extensive experiments on multiple real‐world datasets demonstrate that ESIA‐IDR achieves a 2.21% improvement in NDCG and a 1.48% improvement in Hit Rate compared to the best‐performing baselines, validating its effectiveness in enhancing recommendation performance.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly reshaping the landscape of data-driven research discovery, offering unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding, knowledge synthesis, and intelligent query resolution. This chapter explores the transformative role of LLMs within next-generation research infrastructures, examining how these models augment traditional data pipelines, accelerate hypothesis generation, and enable cross-domain knowledge integration. A proposed methodology integrating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), domain-adaptive fine-tuning, and semantic indexing is presented and evaluated on multi-disciplinary research corpora. Experimental results demonstrate significant gains in retrieval accuracy, citation relevance, and researcher productivity. The chapter further discusses practical advantages, persistent challenges including hallucination and bias, and a forward-looking perspective on human-AI collaborative research ecosystems.

Long COVID syndrome represents a significant public health concern, with healthcare workers constituting a population at particularly high risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and subsequent persistent symptoms. To evaluate the prevalence of Long COVID syndrome in healthcare employees of IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo Foundation over a four-year time window from the pandemic onset. An anonymous survey was conducted among healthcare workers with documented SARS-CoV-2 infection since February 2020. Long COVID syndrome was defined as persistent symptoms lasting beyond 12 weeks from the acute infection, extending to 12 months or more. The Fisher exact test and the McNemar test were used to compare prevalences between groups and over time, respectively. Unsupervised learning techniques were used for identifying patient aggregation. Among 771 respondents (response rate 41.41% of employees with previous SARS-CoV-2 infection), the overall Long COVID syndrome cumulative prevalence (participants experiencing symptoms at any time point) was 27.9% (215/771; 95% CI: 24.7–31.2%), with point prevalence decreasing over time: 26.0% (95% CI 23.0–29.0%) at 3 months, 20.0% (95% CI 17.0–23.0%) at 6 months, and 16.0% (95% CI 14.0–19.0%) at 12 months post-infection. Significant associations were found with job position ( p = 0.004), with nurses showing the highest prevalence (35.0%). Fatigue, joint and muscle pain, concentration troubles, and memory difficulties emerged as the most persistent symptoms over time. Long COVID syndrome affects more than one-quarter of healthcare workers with previous SARS-CoV-2 infection, with symptom persistence demonstrating a gradual decline over time. These findings have important implications for occupational health management and workforce planning in healthcare settings.

Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a “machine psychology” for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

Under the background of the "Healthy China" initiative and the continuous improvement of the occupational health system, pneumoconiosis still poses a challenge to the health rights and interests of workers and the ability of public governance. This disease has the characteristics of long incubation period, irreversible course, and difficult traceability of responsibility. This article reviews the experience of the United States and other developed countries in the control of pneumoconiosis, and uses the panel data of 31 provincial administrative units in China from 2007 to 2023 to construct a two-way fixed effect model. Given data limitations, the reported incidence rate of tuberculosis is used as a proxy indicator to examine macro-level factors such as industrial structure, industrial pollution, public services, labor protection, and medical resources. The study also analyzes institutional inflection points in China’s governance of pneumoconiosis by combining policy documents with prosecutorial case studies. The study found that the share of the secondary sector and sulfur dioxide emissions is significantly and positively correlated with reported incidence rates, while the share of healthcare expenditure, urbanization rates, and infrastructure are significantly and negatively correlated. The relationship between the number of workers covered by work-related injury insurance, the allocation of healthcare professionals, and human capital lacks stability. Case studies further indicate that the coordination among workplace protection, occupational health records, occupational disease diagnosis, work-related injury determination, and benefit payments is a key institutional condition affecting the prevention of pneumoconiosis and the protection of patients. Based on these findings, this paper proposes that the development of the pneumoconiosis management system for the 15th Five-Year Plan should strengthen dust control at the source, protection for high-risk populations, grassroots occupational health services, cross-regional information coordination, and long-term collaborative care, thereby promoting the coordinated development of occupational health risk prevention and control and the protection of workers’ rights.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability among older adults and is increasingly recognized as a significant occupational health issue, especially among healthcare workers who are frequently exposed to repetitive knee strain. This study aims to identify the burden of primary knee osteoarthritis (KOA) among healthcare workers at a tertiary care institution in Bangladesh. Objective: The present study aimed to assess the magnitude and associated factors of primary knee osteoarthritis (KOA) among healthcare workers at BMU. Materials and Methods: This cross-sectional study included 185 healthcare workers selected by simple random sampling at BMU. Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) was diagnosed using the 2016 ACR clinical criteria. Data were collected using a modified and Bangla-adapted COPCORD questionnaire, including PHQ-9 and B-HAQ-DI tools. Anthropometric measurements were taken to calculate BMI. Data were analyzed using SPSS v23.0 with appropriate statistical tests; a p-value <0.05 was considered significant. Results: Among 185 healthcare workers, 42.2% were diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA), and 40% had a B-HAQ-DI score ≥0.8, indicating functional disability. Most KOA cases (57.7%) were female, and mild disability was the most common severity (28.9%). KOA prevalence was similar across physicians (40.5%), nurses (43.1%), and supporting staff (44%). Age was significantly associated with KOA (p = 0.034), with the highest prevalence in the 41–50 age group. Logistic regression identified increasing age (OR 1.064, p = 0.003) and female sex (OR 2.153, p = 0.020) as independent predictors. Conclusion: Knee osteoarthritis was prevalent among healthcare workers, with age and female sex as key predictors, highlighting the need for early intervention and preventive strategies in this population J Dhaka National Med.
